lessons.title: Japan: The Tokyo Stock Exchange, the Nikkei 225, and the Long Road Back

children.text: On 29 December 1989, Japan's Nikkei 225 closed at 38,915.87. Japan was the world's rising economic superpower, Tokyo land was said to be worth more than all of California, and Japanese companies dominated global rankings. Then the bubble burst. The Nikkei did not close above that 1989 peak again until 22 February 2024, more than 34 years later. Imagine buying a Sensex index fund and waiting until your grandchildren were adults just to get your money back. Yet today Japan is one of the most exciting stories in global markets. The Nikkei crossed 50,000 in October 2025 and closed at 64,011.34 on 11 September 2026. This lesson explains both the fall and the comeback.

body.text: Japan proves two things every investor should remember. A great economy full of world-class companies can deliver decades of zero returns if you buy at bubble prices. And governance reform can revive a market that everyone had written off.

body.title: How deep was the fall?
body.prompt: The Nikkei 225 fell from its closing peak of 38,915.87 in December 1989 to a closing low of 7,054.98 in March 2009. What was the total fall, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Fall = (1 − 7,054.98 ÷ 38,915.87) × 100 = (1 − 0.1813) × 100 = 81.9%. A ₹1 lakh investment at the peak would have shrunk to about ₹18,130 at the low. To get back to ₹1 lakh from there, it would need to rise about 452%. Deep falls need enormous recoveries.

body.caption: Compound annual growth rate, the true yearly return over a long period

body.title: The price of buying at the top
body.prompt: Someone bought the Nikkei 225 at its December 1989 close of 38,915.87 and held until the 11 September 2026 close of 64,011.34, a period of about 36.7 years. What was the compound annual price return, in percent? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Ratio = 64,011.34 ÷ 38,915.87 = 1.6449. CAGR = 1.6449^(1 ÷ 36.7) − 1 = about 1.37% a year. Dividends would add a little, but this is still a painful result for more than three and a half decades. Even a bank fixed deposit would have done far better. The lesson is not that Japan is a bad market. It is that the price you pay decides your return.

children.text: Why the Road Was So Long

markDefs.definition: When companies hold shares in each other, often banks, suppliers and customers within the same business group. It protects management from outside shareholders but ties up capital and weakens accountability.
A sustained fall in the general price level. It discourages spending and investment because people expect goods to be cheaper later, and it makes debts heavier in real terms.

children.text: Japan's 1980s boom was built on cheap credit and soaring land prices, and Japanese stocks traded at valuations far above other developed markets. When the Bank of Japan raised rates and the bubble burst, banks were left with mountains of bad loans that took more than a decade to clean up. The economy slipped into
deflation
, companies hoarded cash instead of investing or paying shareholders, and a web of
cross-shareholdings
let managers ignore outside investors. The result became known as Japan's "lost decades".

body.text: Do not assume a market must recover within a few years. Indian investors have grown used to fast rebounds after crashes, such as the Nifty's recovery after March 2020. Japan shows that when a market starts from extreme valuations and faces a banking crisis, deflation and weak governance, recovery can take decades. Diversification and valuation discipline are your protection.

children.text: The Tokyo Stock Exchange Today

The Tokyo Stock Exchange is run by Japan Exchange Group (JPX), whose listed companies were worth about $7.59 trillion in March 2026, making it one of the five largest exchange groups in the world. In April 2022, TSE reorganised its markets into three segments: Prime for large, globally investable companies, Standard for mid-sized companies and Growth for young, high-growth firms. A few trading rules will feel unfamiliar to Indian investors.

body.title: Tokyo after lunch
body.textWithBlank: The Tokyo Stock Exchange resumes trading after its lunch break at 12:30 pm Japan time, which is ___ IST.
body.explanation: Japan is 3 hours 30 minutes ahead of India and does not use daylight saving time. So 12:30 pm JST is 9:00 am IST. Tokyo's afternoon session begins just before NSE's pre-open ends at 9:15 am, which is why Japanese market moves feed straight into the Nifty's opening.

children.text: Nikkei 225 vs TOPIX: Two Very Different Indices

markDefs.definition: The Nikkei 225 divided by the TOPIX. A rising NT ratio means the price-weighted Nikkei is beating the broader market, usually because a few high-priced stocks such as chip companies are rallying.

children.text: The Nikkei 225, run by the Nikkei newspaper group, is the famous headline number. But like the Dow Jones, it is price-weighted. High-priced stocks such as Tokyo Electron, Fast Retailing (the owner of Uniqlo), Advantest and SoftBank Group dominate its moves, and Tokyo Electron alone has had a weight of around 10%. Toyota, Japan's most valuable company, has far less influence because its share price is relatively low. The TOPIX, run by JPX, is weighted by free-float market cap and covers a much broader set of companies, so it gives more weight to banks, carmakers and trading houses. Professionals watch the
NT ratio
to see which is leading.

body.title: Read the split
body.question: One morning the Nikkei 225 rises 2.5% while the TOPIX rises only 0.8%. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A rally in high-priced chip stocks such as Tokyo Electron and Advantest, which carry large weights in the price-weighted Nikkei
Toyota's share price jumped after strong car sales
A calculation error, since both indices track the same stocks in the same way
body.explanation: When the price-weighted Nikkei beats the market cap-weighted TOPIX by a wide margin, the driver is usually a handful of high-priced technology stocks. A bank or Toyota rally would lift the TOPIX more, because those stocks have larger market caps but relatively low share prices. The NT ratio would rise on a day like this.

children.text: The Comeback: A Governance Revolution

Japan's revival is not just about a weaker yen or AI-driven chip stocks. It is about companies finally being pushed to use shareholders' money well. Japan introduced a Stewardship Code for investors in 2014 and a Corporate Governance Code in 2015. Then, in March 2023, the Tokyo Stock Exchange did something unusual for an exchange: it asked listed companies, especially those trading below book value, to disclose plans to improve their capital efficiency and share prices. By the end of 2024, about 90% of Prime companies had published or were preparing such plans. Buybacks surged, cross-shareholdings began to unwind and activist investors grew bolder.

body.title: Buffett's Japan bet
body.prompt: By the end of 2025, Berkshire Hathaway had invested about $15.4 billion in Japan's five big trading houses, and the holdings were worth about $35.4 billion. What was the percentage gain on cost, excluding dividends? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Gain = ($35.4 billion ÷ $15.4 billion − 1) × 100 = (2.2987 − 1) × 100 = 129.9%. Berkshire began buying in 2020, when these companies traded at low valuations, paid steady dividends and were starting to return more cash to shareholders. It is a textbook example of buying good businesses at cheap prices just before governance and profitability improve.

body.text: Notice the difference between Japan in 1989 and Japan in 2020. The companies were often the same, but in 1989 investors paid bubble valuations for them, and in 2020 many traded below book value. The same business can be a terrible or brilliant investment depending on the price and on whether management starts treating shareholders better.

children.text: The Yen: Japan's Other Market Driver

markDefs.definition: Borrowing in a low-interest currency, historically the yen, to invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere. When the funding currency suddenly strengthens or its interest rates rise, traders rush to unwind these positions, which can trigger sharp global sell-offs.

children.text: Japan's biggest companies, from Toyota to Sony, earn heavily abroad, so a weak yen boosts their profits and a strong yen hurts them. For years, near-zero Japanese interest rates also made the yen the world's favourite funding currency for the
carry trade

. That changed as the Bank of Japan ended negative interest rates in March 2024 and kept raising them. When the yen surged in early August 2024, carry trades unwound violently. On 5 August 2024, the Nikkei 225 crashed 12.4%, its worst day since 1987, and the Nifty 50 fell 2.68%. In mid-September 2026, USD/JPY was around 154, with markets expecting more BOJ hikes.

body.title: Japanese gains, rupee returns
body.prompt: Illustrative figures: a Japan-focused fund rises 20% in yen over a year, but the yen weakens 10% against the rupee over the same period. Using (1 + fund return) × (1 + currency change) − 1, what is the return in rupees, in percent?
body.explanation: Return in ₹ = (1 + 0.20) × (1 − 0.10) − 1 = 1.20 × 0.90 − 1 = 1.08 − 1 = 8%. More than half of the local gain disappears in rupee terms. This is exactly what happened to many foreign investors in Japan during periods of rapid yen weakness: a strong Nikkei, but a much weaker return at home.

children.text: Japan and India: Closer Than You Think

Japanese companies are among the most important foreign owners of Indian listed businesses, and Japan's big banks have made record bets on Indian finance. Japanese deals in India topped $9 billion in 2025, with finance as the main target. When you track Maruti Suzuki, Yes Bank or Shriram Finance, you are partly tracking Japanese corporate strategy.

body.title: An early morning yen shock
body.scenario: At 5:30 am IST on a Tuesday, the Nikkei 225 opens 5% lower. Overnight, a senior Bank of Japan official hinted at a faster pace of rate hikes, and the yen has jumped 3% against the dollar. GIFT Nifty is down 1.2%. You hold Maruti Suzuki, Infosys and HDFC Bank shares, and a Nifty 50 index fund.
body.prompt: Explain what is likely happening in global markets, how it could reach Indian stocks by 9:15 am, and what you should check before reacting.
body.modelAnswer:
What is happening:
1. A hawkish BOJ signal is strengthening the yen. Japanese exporters fall because a strong yen shrinks their overseas profits in yen terms.
2. Traders who borrowed in yen to buy higher-yielding assets may be unwinding carry trades, selling risky assets worldwide, including emerging market stocks.

How it reaches India:
1. Mood: GIFT Nifty is already signalling a weaker open, as on 5 August 2024, when the Nikkei fell 12.4% and the Nifty 2.68%.
2. Money: If carry trades unwind broadly, FPIs may sell Indian large caps such as HDFC Bank.
3. Maruti Suzuki: Its parent Suzuki is Japanese, but Maruti earns mostly in rupees. It may dip with the market, though a strong yen can also raise the rupee cost of some imported parts.
4. Infosys: Likely to follow global tech sentiment rather than the yen directly.

What to check: how far USD/JPY has moved, whether US futures are also falling, FPI flow data, and whether the Nikkei is stabilising by its lunch break at 8:00 am IST. Avoid panic selling at the open. One-day carry trade shocks have often reversed partly within days, but confirm before acting.

body.title: Your early morning Japan check
steps: At 5:30 am IST, note the Nikkei 225 and TOPIX openings and compare the two.
Check USD/JPY. A sharp yen surge is a warning sign for carry trade unwinding.
Look at the big Nikkei movers such as Tokyo Electron and Advantest for signals on global chip stocks.
Note any Bank of Japan news or comments from officials.
At 8:00 am IST, when Tokyo breaks for lunch, check whether the move has deepened or stabilised, then look at GIFT Nifty.

cards.definition: Japan's headline price-weighted index of 225 stocks, run by Nikkei Inc. It peaked at 38,915.87 in 1989 and regained that level only in February 2024.
A broad, free-float market cap-weighted index of Tokyo-listed companies, run by JPX and used as the main institutional benchmark.
Nikkei 225 divided by TOPIX. A rising ratio means high-priced stocks are leading the broader market.
The Tokyo Stock Exchange's top segment for large, globally investable companies, created in April 2022.
Companies owning each other's shares, a long-standing Japanese practice that reforms are now unwinding.
Borrowing cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere. Its sudden unwinding caused the Nikkei's 12.4% crash on 5 August 2024.
Compound annual growth rate. Buying the Nikkei at the 1989 peak and holding to September 2026 produced only about 1.37% a year in price terms.

points: The Nikkei 225 peaked at 38,915.87 in December 1989, fell 81.9% to its 2009 low, and did not beat its old peak until February 2024.
Buying at the 1989 top and holding to September 2026 returned only about 1.37% a year in price terms. The price you pay matters enormously.
The Tokyo Stock Exchange has a lunch break, trades in 100-share units and settles on T+2. In IST, it trades from 5:30 am to 8:00 am and 9:00 am to 12:00 noon.
The Nikkei 225 is price-weighted and tilted to high-priced chip and tech stocks. TOPIX is market cap-weighted and broader.
Japan's comeback is driven by governance reform, including TSE's 2023 capital efficiency request and record buybacks of ¥22.32 trillion in fiscal 2025.
The yen and BOJ policy are critical. The BOJ rate reached 1.00% in 2026, and the yen carry trade unwind caused a 12.4% Nikkei crash on 5 August 2024.
Japan is deeply tied to India through Suzuki's stake in Maruti Suzuki, SMBC's stake in Yes Bank and MUFG's 20% stake in Shriram Finance.
